title: Ruth and Jonah
intro: 20 days through two short Bible stories, Ruth and Jonah, one verse at a time.

posts.caption: Starting today, 20 days through two of the Bible's shortest stories: Ruth, then Jonah. Ruth opens with loss: in the time of the judges, before Israel had kings, famine drives one family out of Bethlehem, whose name means "house of bread," to Moab, a neighboring nation east of the Dead Sea. Many readers sum up the book's theme with the Hebrew word hesed, loyal love, which carries this family from emptiness to hope.

Naomi's husband and both sons have died in Moab, and she is going home to Bethlehem. She urges her two widowed Moabite daughters-in-law to go back to their own families. Orpah does, but Ruth refuses with these words, binding herself to Naomi, her people and her God. Jewish tradition honors Ruth as the model of someone who joins the Jewish people by choice. The words are often read at weddings, though Ruth spoke them to her mother-in-law.

Naomi arrives back in Bethlehem, and the town's women can hardly believe it's her. She left with a husband and two sons and has come back with only Ruth, and she says plainly that God has made her life bitter. In Hebrew, Naomi means "pleasant" and Mara means "bitter." The book lets her grief stand without correcting it. "The Almighty" translates Shaddai, an ancient name for God.

Israel's law told farmers to leave dropped grain for the poor, widows and foreigners to gather, a practice called gleaning, and Ruth is all three. She just "happens" to pick a field owned by Boaz, a relative of Naomi's late husband. He tells her to stay close and drink from his workers' water jars, and his kindness to a foreigner leaves her astonished.

Boaz, the landowner, has heard how Ruth left her own parents and homeland to stay with Naomi, and he blesses her. He pictures her as sheltering under the wings of Israel's God, like a young bird, and prays that God will reward her loyalty. The Hebrew word for "wings," kanaf, also means the corner or edge of a garment, and it returns at a key moment in the next chapter, when Boaz himself becomes part of the answer.

Ruth comes home with a big load of barley, and Naomi learns the field belongs to Boaz, one of their kinsman-redeemers (go'el in Hebrew): close relatives responsible for rescuing family in trouble. Back in chapter 1, Naomi prayed that her daughters-in-law would find rest in the home of a new husband. Now she sets out to make that happen for Ruth.

On Naomi's advice, Ruth goes at night to the threshing floor, where Boaz sleeps after the harvest, and lies down at his feet. When he wakes, startled, she makes a bold request: that he spread the corner of his garment over her, a way of asking for marriage and protection (compare Ezekiel 16:8). The Hebrew for "corner," kanaf, is the same word as the "wings" in Boaz's blessing on her, so, commentators note, Boaz can become the answer to his own prayer.

Boaz agrees to Ruth's request, though a closer relative has the first right to redeem. His reason is her character: the whole town knows she is "a woman of noble character," a remarkable tribute to a foreign widow. In Hebrew it is eshet chayil, the same phrase that opens the poem at the end of Proverbs (31:10), and in some Hebrew Bibles Ruth comes right after Proverbs. The narrator used a matching phrase for Boaz in chapter 2.

Boaz settles the matter at the town gate, marries Ruth, and they have a son. The women of Bethlehem, who heard Naomi call herself empty, now celebrate with her. Seven was a number of completeness, and sons meant security in old age, so this is very high praise for a foreign daughter-in-law.

The twist at the end: Ruth, the outsider from Moab, becomes the great-grandmother of King David. Matthew's Gospel later names her in the family line of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). Jews traditionally read the book of Ruth at Shavuot, the early-summer festival of the wheat harvest. That's Ruth; Jonah comes next.

From Ruth we turn to Jonah, a very different short story. Jonah, whose name means "dove," is a prophet also mentioned in 2 Kings 14:25. God sends him to Nineveh, a great city of Assyria, Israel's feared enemy, whose ruins lie in Mosul, Iraq. Instead he sails from Joppa for Tarshish, a distant port in the opposite direction, possibly in Spain.

God sends a violent storm, and the terrified sailors cast lots to find out who is to blame. The lot falls on Jonah, and this is his answer. The irony is hard to miss: he worships the God who made the sea, and he is trying to escape that God by sea.

The storm keeps getting worse, and Jonah tells the sailors to throw him overboard. Instead they row hard for land, and they pray to Jonah's God before they finally do it. Many readers notice that these foreign sailors come across as more decent, and more open to God, than the prophet himself.

Thrown overboard, Jonah should drown, but God "appoints" a great fish to swallow him, and it becomes a rescue rather than a death. The Hebrew says "a great fish," not a whale; the whale came later through translations like the King James Version, which says "whale" in Matthew 12:40, where Jesus compares his own three days in the grave to Jonah's. In Hebrew Bibles, this verse is numbered as the first verse of chapter 2.

From inside the fish, Jonah finally turns to God. His prayer is written as a psalm of thanks, and its point is simple: even from the depths, after running away, he called and God answered. Several lines echo the book of Psalms (compare Psalm 120:1). Sheol is the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead, so Jonah describes himself as already as good as dead. At the end of the prayer, the fish spits him out onto dry land.

God tells Jonah a second time to go, and this time he does. His message is a bare warning, just five words in Hebrew, with no call to repent and no word of mercy. The verb for "overturned" is the one used for the destruction of Sodom, but it can also mean "turned around" or "changed," a double meaning many readers notice once they see how the story ends.

Nineveh listens. The king trades his robe for sackcloth and orders a fast for people and even animals, saying, "Who knows? God may turn and relent." God sees that they have truly changed their ways and spares the city. Many readers see this as the warning's purpose all along: to turn the city around, not simply to destroy it. Jonah is read in synagogues on the afternoon of Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, whose theme is repentance.

posts.display: “This is why I was so quick to flee toward Tarshish. I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion—One who relents from sending disaster.”
posts.caption: Instead of celebrating, Jonah is furious, and now he explains why he ran in the first place. He echoes God's description of himself to Moses in Exodus 34:6, one of the most repeated lines in the Hebrew Bible. By his own account, Jonah fled because he expected God to forgive Nineveh.

Jonah is so angry at God's mercy to Nineveh that he asks to die. God doesn't scold him; he asks a question, inviting Jonah to look honestly at his anger. Jonah doesn't reply. He camps outside the city, and God "appoints" a plant to shade him, then a worm to kill it, then a scorching wind, the same verb used for the great fish. Then God asks the same question again, this time about the plant.

Jonah is angry that his shade plant died, and God answers with this question: if Jonah cares about a plant, shouldn't God care about a whole city of people, and even its animals? The book ends right there, without Jonah's reply, leaving the question with the reader. Those who "cannot tell their right hand from their left" may mean small children, or people without moral guidance. That's Ruth and Jonah. Thank you for reading them with me.
